newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong steps up anti-Japan campaign over isles.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong steps up anti-Japan campaign over isles.

text.p: Indignant Hong Kong activists on Saturday stepped up campaigns against Japan's claims to a group of disputed islands in the East China Sea.
Japan has stoked outrage in the British territory by reasserting its claim to the Diaoyu Islands and stationing naval forces in its surrounding sea, after Japanese erected a lighthouse on the isles.
The islands, which lie about 190 miles west of the Japanese island of Okinawa, are also claimed by Beijing and Taipei.
Hong Kong's population, which consists mainly of ethnic Chinese, believes the islands belong to China.
Tokyo's moves have rekindled fears of Japanese militarism in Hong Kong residents, who remember with bitter memories the atrocities committed by Japan against the Chinese during World War Two.

Activists from across the politicial spectrum in Hong Kong, which is set to revert to Chinese sovereignty next year, have been staging protests against Japan, particularly over its stance on the islands, which are known as Senkakus in Japanese.
The campaigns escalated on Saturday when activists handed out leaflets near a Japanese department store in the bustling Causeway Bay commercial area, urging shoppers to boycott Japanese goods.
"After the rape of Nanjing, it is unthinkable that the Japanese are doing such a thing. The whole world has forgotten what they have done in World War Two," said a furious passer-by.
Japanese soldiers killed hundreds of thousands of Chinese in a massacre in the southern city of Nanjing in 1937.

Another group, which has called on Chinese all over the world to protest against Japan's presence on the islands, is lobbying for a fresh boycott of Japanese goods on September 18, the anniversary of Japan's invasion of China in 1931.
"Against Japanese militarism", some banner-brandishing protesters chanted as they marched to the Chung Hwa Travel Service and the Xinhua news agency, the de facto Taiwanese and Chinese consulates.
They petitioned China and Taiwan to take a firm stance against Japan over the sovereignty of the Diaoyu islands and to protect their fishermen near the islands now monitored by the Japanese navy.
Other demonstrators marched to the Japanese consulate.
Some activists launched a petition to urge Japan to demolish the lighthouse from the islands and to apologise for its repeated claim to the islands.
One group confirmed its plan to sail to the islands on October 5 to remove the lighthouse, after securing a boat and 70 participants.
Local media have carried anti-Japan campaigns, while newspapers and radio talk show have criticised Japanese aggression.
Journalists from two television stations and two newspapers here had been barred from the islands by the Japanese navy.
The wave of anger flared amid Hong Kong's highly charged political atmosphere in less than 300 days before the British colony reverts to China at midnight on June 30, 1997.
Outside the office of a China-appointed panel overseeing the handover, a group protested over the "undemocratic" way in which a caucus to choose Hong Kong's post-handover leader will be formed.
